paragraphs.ncert_ref: Equilibrium: the law of mass action and K
paragraphs.key_phrase: the ratio settles, the amounts do not have to
paragraphs.meaning: At equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions run at the same rate, so concentrations stop changing even though both reactions continue. The law of mass action turns that into an expression: products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient, gives a constant at a given temperature. K does not depend on the starting amounts, only on temperature and the reaction itself.

words.meaning: The value of the products-over-reactants ratio at equilibrium, for a given temperature.
words.breakdown: Kc uses concentrations, Kp uses partial pressures. Solids and pure liquids are left out.
words.trap: K is not a rate constant. It says where the balance lies, not how fast it is reached.

words.meaning: A state where both reactions continue at equal rates, so nothing appears to change.
words.breakdown: It needs a closed system, otherwise products escape and the balance shifts.
words.trap: Equilibrium is not the point where the reaction stops. Labelling molecules would show both directions still running.

words.meaning: The equilibrium constant written with partial pressures or with concentrations.
words.breakdown: They are related by Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, where Δn is the change in moles of gas.
words.trap: When Δn is zero the two are equal. Writing a conversion factor then is unnecessary but harmless; getting Δn wrong is not.

paragraphs.visual_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 150'><path class='d-line' d='M30 118h260M30 118V32'/><path class='d-accent' d='M36 44l70 40'/><path class='d-muted' d='M36 110l70-26'/><circle class='d-fill' cx='116' cy='86' r='4'/><path class='d-guide' d='M116 86V118'/><text class='d-label' x='124' y='70'>forward</text><text class='d-label' x='124' y='108'>reverse</text><text class='d-label' x='76' y='134'>rates equal here</text></svg>
paragraphs.visual_alt: Forward and reverse rate curves meeting and staying equal at equilibrium.
paragraphs.hook: Nothing changes at equilibrium except that everything is still changing.
paragraphs.exam_note: Writing K correctly is the mark: products on top, coefficients as powers, pure solids and liquids omitted. K for a reversed reaction is 1/K.
paragraphs.trap: Doubling a reaction squares its K, and halving it takes the square root. The exponent follows the coefficients you write.

recall.q: If the equation is reversed, the equilibrium constant becomes
recall.why: Reversing swaps products and reactants, so the ratio is inverted and K becomes 1/K.

recall.q: Pure solids are omitted from the equilibrium expression because
recall.why: The amount of a pure solid per unit volume does not change, so it folds into the constant instead of appearing in the ratio.

paragraphs.review_note: Verify page and line against your edition, and check the Kp and Kc relation against your copy.

paragraphs.ncert_ref: Equilibrium: predicting the direction of change
paragraphs.meaning: The reaction quotient Q has exactly the same form as K, but is calculated with the concentrations at this moment, not at equilibrium. If Q is smaller than K the reaction must make more products, so it moves forward; if Q is larger it moves back. Equilibrium is simply the case where the two numbers are equal.

words.meaning: The products-over-reactants ratio at any moment, not necessarily at equilibrium.
words.breakdown: Q uses current concentrations; K uses equilibrium ones.
words.trap: Q is not sprinkled on the answer. It is a test value, and the comparison with K is the whole point.

words.meaning: Net reaction in the forward direction, producing more products.
words.breakdown: Happens when Q is less than K.
words.trap: A shift right does not mean the reverse reaction stops. Both continue, at unequal rates.

words.meaning: The same ratio written with partial pressures.
words.breakdown: Compare Qp with Kp, and Qc with Kc; do not mix the two.
words.trap: Comparing a pressure quotient with a concentration constant is meaningless unless you convert one of them first.

paragraphs.visual_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 150'><path class='d-line' d='M40 118h240M40 118V32'/><path class='d-accent' d='M60 100h200'/><circle class='d-fill' cx='110' cy='100' r='5'/><circle class='d-fill' cx='210' cy='100' r='5'/><text class='d-label' x='78' y='84'>Q below K</text><text class='d-label' x='178' y='84'>Q above K</text><text class='d-label' x='78' y='134'>runs forward</text><text class='d-label' x='178' y='134'>runs backward</text></svg>
paragraphs.visual_alt: A number line of Q with K marked, showing forward reaction below K and reverse above it.
paragraphs.hook: Q is where you are. K is where you are going.
paragraphs.exam_note: Questions give initial concentrations and ask the direction. Compute Q, compare with K, and state the direction in words.
paragraphs.trap: The comparison is with the same temperature's K. Using a K from a different temperature gives the wrong direction.

recall.q: If Q is less than K, the reaction
recall.why: Too few products are present relative to the equilibrium ratio, so the forward reaction must run to raise Q towards K.
At equilibrium the current ratio is the equilibrium ratio, so the two values are identical.

paragraphs.review_note: Verify page and line against your edition, and check the direction criterion against your copy.

paragraphs.meaning: Le Chatelier's principle says that when a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it shifts in the direction that reduces the disturbance. Adding a reactant pushes the reaction forward, raising the pressure favours the side with fewer gas molecules, and heating favours the endothermic direction. A catalyst does none of these things: it only shortens the time taken to reach the same equilibrium.

words.meaning: A system at equilibrium shifts to oppose any change imposed on it.
words.breakdown: Changes in concentration, pressure, volume or temperature all count.
words.trap: A catalyst is not on this list. It changes the rate, never the position of equilibrium.

words.meaning: The direction of reaction that releases heat.
words.breakdown: Cooling favours it; heating favours the endothermic direction.
words.trap: Heating does not always push the reaction forward. It pushes it in the endothermic direction, whichever side that is.

words.meaning: A change in total pressure that shifts the side with fewer gas moles when pressure rises.
words.breakdown: Only gases count, and only when the numbers of gas moles differ on the two sides.
words.trap: Adding an inert gas at constant volume changes nothing, because the partial pressures of the reacting gases are unchanged.

paragraphs.visual_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 150'><path class='d-line' d='M30 118h260'/><rect class='d-line' x='70' y='46' width='60' height='40' rx='2'/><path class='d-accent' d='M134 66h22M150 58l10 8-10 8'/><rect class='d-line' x='160' y='56' width='60' height='20' rx='2'/><text class='d-label' x='70' y='104'>2 gas moles</text><text class='d-label' x='160' y='104'>1 gas mole</text><text class='d-label' x='70' y='34'>raise pressure: shift right</text></svg>
paragraphs.visual_alt: Two sides of a reaction with different numbers of gas moles, with an arrow showing a pressure increase shifting to the side with fewer.
paragraphs.hook: Squeeze a gas equilibrium and it moves to the side with less room taken up.
paragraphs.exam_note: The Haber process is the standard case: high pressure and moderate temperature, with the compromise explained by rate against yield.
paragraphs.trap: Pressure increase does not always shift right. It shifts towards fewer gas moles, which may be the reactant side.

recall.q: Adding a catalyst to a system at equilibrium
options: Changes neither the position nor K
recall.why: A catalyst speeds both directions equally, so the system reaches the same equilibrium sooner but does not move it.

recall.q: For an exothermic reaction at equilibrium, raising the temperature
recall.why: Heating favours the endothermic direction, which is the reverse for an exothermic reaction, so K falls.

paragraphs.review_note: Verify page and line against your edition, and check the Haber conditions against your copy.

paragraphs.ncert_ref: Equilibrium: ionic equilibrium, pH and buffers
paragraphs.key_phrase: pH is minus log of hydrogen ion concentration
paragraphs.meaning: Water ionises slightly, and the product of hydrogen and hydroxide ion concentrations is 10^-14 at room temperature. That single number defines pH and links acids and bases: adding acid raises hydrogen ion concentration and lowers pH. A buffer resists that change because it contains both a weak acid and its conjugate base, so added acid is consumed by the base and added base by the acid.

words.meaning: The negative logarithm of the hydrogen ion concentration.
words.breakdown: pH 7 is neutral at 25 °C, below 7 acidic, above 7 basic.
words.trap: pH 7 is neutral only near 25 °C. At higher temperatures the neutral point is slightly below 7.

words.meaning: A solution that resists a change in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added.
words.breakdown: Usually a weak acid with its salt, or a weak base with its salt.
words.trap: A buffer is not unlimited. Adding enough acid exhausts the base component and the pH then falls sharply.

words.meaning: The product of ion concentrations in a saturated solution of a sparingly soluble salt.
words.breakdown: Ksp for silver chloride is the product of silver and chloride ion concentrations.
words.trap: Ksp is not a solubility in grams per litre. It is an ion product, and its units depend on the salt.

paragraphs.visual_svg: <svg viewBox='0 0 320 150'><path class='d-line' d='M30 116h260M30 116V32'/><path class='d-accent' d='M40 108h90'/><path class='d-accent' d='M146 108v-30c0-12 30-12 30 0v30'/><path class='d-muted' d='M202 108c0-40 24-58 52-66'/><text class='d-label' x='40' y='126'>add acid</text><text class='d-label' x='150' y='70'>buffer holds</text><text class='d-label' x='200' y='36'>no buffer: pH falls</text></svg>
paragraphs.visual_alt: A pH curve that stays flat with a buffer and drops sharply without one as acid is added.
paragraphs.hook: A buffer does not stop the acid. It spends itself soaking it up.
paragraphs.exam_note: Buffer pH uses the Henderson equation, pH equals pKa plus log of salt over acid. The ratio matters, not the absolute amounts.
paragraphs.trap: A strong acid has a very low pH but not a negative one in normal solutions. Concentrated acids are still below pH 1 only in extreme cases.

recall.q: A solution of pH 3 has a hydrogen ion concentration of
recall.why: pH is minus log of the hydrogen ion concentration, so pH 3 means 10 to the power minus 3 molar.

recall.q: A buffer works because it contains
options: A weak acid and its conjugate base
recall.why: Both components are needed so that added acid is neutralised by the base and added base by the acid.
